Great Salt Lake at Risk of Drying Up After Massive Data Center Approved

Data centers are the backbone of everything online cloud storage, streaming, AI, banking systems, and social media. But behind the screens is a huge physical footprint that many people don’t realize. A single large data center can use 300,000 to over 5 million gallons of water per day just to cool the servers. Some of the biggest facilities use as much water as a town of 30,000–50,000 people, and this demand is rising every year as more companies expand their digital infrastructure.

This is where the Great Lakes come into the picture. The Great Lakes hold 20% of the world’s fresh surface water, making the region extremely attractive to corporations looking for reliable, inexpensive, long-term water supplies. While Western states face droughts and restrictions, Michigan and surrounding areas still have large water reserves, cooler temperatures, and lower land costs. To big tech companies, it looks like the perfect place to build.

But high water use comes with high consequences.

Most data centers cool servers using evaporative cooling, which means the water they take in doesn’t go back to the lake it evaporates into the air and leaves the watershed entirely. Other cooling systems pump water back out, but that water is significantly warmer, contributing to thermal pollution. Warmer water can harm fish populations, disrupt breeding cycles, damage cold-water species, and change lake ecosystems in ways that are hard to reverse. Water used for cooling often contains chemical additives like biocides and anti-corrosion agents. If these aren’t carefully handled, they pose additional environmental risks.

Then there’s the energy problem. Data centers use massive power as much electricity as a factory or small city. This increased demand forces utilities to expand infrastructure or build new power sources, often relying on fossil fuels. In many cases, residents end up absorbing these costs through higher energy rates, even though the data center benefits the most. And while companies often promise economic growth, a typical data center only creates 35–100 permanent jobs, far fewer than what local communities expect after offering huge tax breaks.

There’s also concern about groundwater. While the Great Lakes appear endless, the aquifers beneath them are not. Heavy industrial water withdrawals, combined with climate change, can lower water tables in surrounding towns and rural communities. Once groundwater levels drop, they may never fully return to normal.

Supporters argue that data centers are necessary for economic development, but critics warn that Michigan must proceed cautiously. The Great Lakes Compact protects the basin from excessive water exports, but it does not fully regulate how much water companies can withdraw for industrial use as long as it technically stays within the watershed. Meanwhile, long-term environmental monitoring, public transparency, and community benefits agreements are often minimal.

The bottom line: Data centers provide digital convenience, but they come with enormous water and energy costs. With the Great Lakes being one of the most important freshwater systems on Earth, Michigan has a responsibility to ensure these resources aren’t treated as a limitless corporate cooling supply. The lakes belong to the people not private companies looking for cheap water.

A plan to create one of the world’s largest datacentres in the US state of Utah has provoked a furious public backlash amid concerns over its vast energy use and impact upon the state’s stressed water supplies.⁠
⁠
The Stratos artificial intelligence datacentre footprint would cover more than 40,000 acres (160 sq km) over three sites in Box Elder county in north-western Utah. The facility will suck up a significant amount of water in an area that has been hit by severe drought in recent years, and is expected to raise the state’s planet-heating pollution by about 50% by consuming a huge amount of energy and water to power and cool itself, according to one impact analysis.
⁠
Last week, the project was approved by the county’s commissioners, despite thousands of objections lodged by Utah residents. Environmentalists have warned that Stratos could imperil the Great Salt Lake ecosystem, including a critical migratory bird habitat, which is already under severe stress.⁠
⁠
The proposed project is backed by the venture capitalist Kevin O’Leary, who has claimed Stratos will deliver thousands of jobs. But these jobs will not outweigh the longer-term impacts to Utah and beyond, critics argue.⁠
⁠
“This has all the hallmarks of an out-of-state megaproject with little to no concern for the local community,” said Ben Abbott, an ecologist at Brigham Young University and executive director of Grow the Flow, a group that aims to protect the Great Salt Lake.
⁠

My take on this went viral on Instagram. Then a friend reached out and sent me a video by @lthlnkso (Quick Thoughts on X). He breaks down the concerns and offers powerful alternate views everyone should hear before forming an opinion.

"It'll use double Utah's electricity!" True. But the entire power plant is being built on-site, just for this data center. It's not pulling from Utah's grid. Not raising electric bills for residents. For context, Texas already uses 10x what Utah uses. Pennsylvania uses 4x. This project doesn't change anyone's bill.

"It'll drain all the water!" The water in Hansel Valley already grows alfalfa. A crop so water-hungry it consumes 79% of all Colorado River water in the West. A lot of that alfalfa gets exported overseas to feed cattle in Saudi Arabia and China. The data center is buying that water from farmers. Same water, different use.

"It'll cook the state alive!" The temperature increase isn't statewide. It's confined to Hansel Valley. Daytime up to 5°F. Nighttime up to 28°F. Trapped in the valley. But Hansel Valley is uninhabited. It's an empty desert. Nobody lives there to feel the heat.

"40,000 acres is insane!" The 40,000 acres isn't all building. That's the project area. Most of it will stay undeveloped. The actual structures sit on a small fraction of the land. They needed the acreage to secure water rights and to keep buffer space around the facility.

But what about the Great Salt Lake? Hansel Valley sits right at the north end of the Great Salt Lake. The lake is at its third-lowest level in history and dying. The data center's heat could accelerate evaporation. This is the most credible criticism of the project, in my opinion. The counter? The lake is dying mostly because agriculture is using all its water. The data center is rerouting that agricultural water. Would love to hear if there's a counter to this potential problem, or something I'm not thinking about.

The bigger picture. Data centers are going to get built somewhere. AI demand is exploding. An uninhabited desert valley with on-site power, repurposed agricultural water, and no nearby homes might be a pretty decent location for a massive data center. Better here than in someone's backyard.
